title: Ask the experts: sourcing a high-quality nutrition counseling dataset through Human-AI collaboration

reviews.summary: The goal of this work is to create a dataset to evaluate the potential for LLMs (here, ChatGPT) to assist in nutritional counseling. To do this, the authors 1) work with nutrition experts to build a framework for what types of content should be present in a conversation about someone's nutritional struggles, 2) crowdsource a set of common nutritional struggles, 3) worked with nutrition experts to engineer a prompt for ChatGPT to provide a supportive response to a nutritional struggle, 4) had nutrition experts annotate ChatGPT supportive responses for content (existing rubric) and safety (new rubric), and 5) interview nutrition experts to get their qualitative perspectives on how ChatGPT did. They released their labeled datasets (2.4K struggles, 97K supportive texts), and provided some baseline stats on prediction tasks and generalization to other LLMs using this data. Overall a great paper!
reviews.strengths:
- The authors treated this (very sensitive) topic with a lot of care and attention.
- The consistent and intentional involvement of nutrition experts in the work is a major strength. The level of detail in Table 10 is fantastic.
- The inclusion of qualitative work -- both in the annotations and in the struggles clustering -- was useful to understanding the data and context.
- Generally, methodological choices were made with a lot of intentionality -- e.g., crowdsourcing of nutrition struggles, creation of prompts and evaluation metrics, etc. 
- I appreciated the clarity of framing in lines 165-169. 
- It was useful to see how ChatGPT compares to other LLMs in Section 8
- The resources provided (new datasets, models, etc.) seem quite useful
reviews.weaknesses:
No huge issues but a few things could be discussed more or clarified:

- In Section 7.1, you show that ChatGPT performs well on your many quantitative metrics (assuming a ~20% unsafe rating is good?) -- but then in Section 7.2, it seems like the experts had many concerns with the outputs. Is it possible that there are metrics that you could have used to capture these concerns quantitatively? For instance, if one of the rubric items had been about usefulness or how well the response was customized to the person would you have potentially seen more scores in the bottom end of the likert range? Are there other items you could have added to the likert block to show quantitatively that there were pervasive issues? I don't think you need to actually do more evaluation but it would be nice to see a solid discussion on some additional items you might add to the rubric in light of your qualitative work.
- The authors reviewed performance by the "type" of struggle the person was dealing with, but did not look at performance based on the demographic attributes of the person with the struggle. For instance, it's not clear if ChatGPT does a better job talking to an educated person, a white person, etc. Could the authors produce charts like these (or speak to such an analysis), given that they have the needed data?
- It wasn't entirely clear to me that you'd written four different prompts for each of the attributes in RQ1 until I read Appendix G. Could you clarify this in Section 6?
- In Section 6 (or Appendix G), could you reflect a little more on the types of issues you were trying to address in the initial prompts?
reviews.questions:
- (minor) In your related work section, you give a handful of examples of papers that use LLMs in nutritional advice (lines 83-89). Could you include a sentence at the end of that paragraph, explaining the contributions your work makes over and above these prior papers?
- (minor) Overall, you did a lot of work to include experts in your process. Can you add some discussion speaking to the value this brought and potentially use your related work to position your expert inclusion in the space of participatory research?
- (minor) Please review the paper for typos and consistency (e.g., the order of the four subparts of RQ1 is not the same in all figures/tables)
